why: Minimum adjacent swaps to turn one arrangement into another equals the number of inversions of the permutation that sends each source character to its target position. Matching the k-th copy of a character in source to the k-th copy in target is optimal (equal characters never need to cross), and inversions are counted with a Fenwick tree in O(n log n).
hints: If every character were distinct, how many adjacent swaps does it take to sort a permutation?

Map each source position to the target position it must reach; for repeated characters, pair them in order (first with first), since swapping two equal characters is wasted. The answer is the inversion count of that position array.
Build perm with a queue of target positions per character, then sweep from the right with a Fenwick tree counting how many smaller positions were already seen. O(n log n), 64-bit result.
pitfalls: Pairing equal characters out of order adds useless crossings and overcounts.
The count can reach about n^2 / 2 = 2 * 10^10, more than 32 bits.
Characters are ASCII, not only letters; key the position queues by character, not by 'a'..'z' index.
